presentingComplaint: Five days of right-sided chest and upper abdominal pain with high fever and rigors, initially treated as chest infection.
history: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 9.4%) on metformin presented with 5 days of fever with rigors and a dull ache in the right upper abdomen radiating to the right shoulder tip. Over the last 48h he developed right-sided pleuritic pain and a dry cough, prompting a primary-care diagnosis of 'right basal pneumonia' and a course of oral amoxicillin, with no improvement. He reports anorexia, nausea, and 3 kg unintentional weight loss over the fortnight. No diarrhoea, no recent travel outside urban India, no dysentery history. Non-drinker. No prior biliary disease or gallstone symptoms.
examination: Ill-looking, mildly dehydrated. Tender hepatomegaly with point tenderness over the lower right intercostal spaces and a positive 'intercostal tenderness' sign. Right basal breath sounds reduced with a small sympathetic pleural effusion; no bronchial breathing or coarse consolidation. Mild scleral icterus. Murphy sign negative. No peritonism.
imaging: Chest X-ray: elevated right hemidiaphragm with small right pleural effusion, no lobar consolidation. Abdominal ultrasound: single 6.4 cm hypoechoic lesion with internal echoes in segment VII/VIII of the right lobe. Contrast CT abdomen: solitary thick-walled, rim-enhancing hypodense hepatic collection with peripheral oedema, no biliary dilatation and normal gallbladder.
microbiology: Ultrasound-guided percutaneous aspiration yielded ~40 mL of thick 'anchovy-sauce'-negative, foul, greenish pus; Gram stain: Gram-negative bacilli. Pus and blood cultures grew Klebsiella pneumoniae (hypermucoviscous, string-test positive), pan-susceptible. Amoebic serology (IHA) negative; stool for E. histolytica antigen negative.
differentialDiagnoses: Right basal community-acquired pneumonia with effusion
finalDiagnosis: Pyogenic (Klebsiella pneumoniae) liver abscess in a poorly controlled diabetic, masquerading as right basal pneumonia
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e - Liver Abscess
stewardship: Empiric IV ceftriaxone plus metronidazole after obtaining blood cultures and pus for culture; combine antibiotics with source control by image-guided percutaneous drainage. Rationale: covers enteric Gram-negative bacilli (including Klebsiella, the dominant organism in diabetic Asian patients), streptococci, and anaerobes, with metronidazole also treating amoebic abscess empirically until serology returns. De-escalate to a narrow agent once susceptibilities are known.
contraindications: Avoid metronidazole with concurrent alcohol (disulfiram-like reaction)
Cap contrast load / monitor renal function given diabetic nephropathy risk
edgeCases: Hypermucoviscous K. pneumoniae liver abscess can seed metastatic infection (endophthalmitis, meningitis) - perform fundoscopy and low threshold for imaging if neurological or ocular symptoms appear
A right basal effusion and pleuritic pain can wrongly anchor to pneumonia and delay abdominal imaging
Negative amoebic serology does not exclude early amoebic abscess but pus culture growing Klebsiella confirms pyogenic aetiology
expectedMaiK: Solitary rim-enhancing hepatic collection with fever, rigors, tender hepatomegaly, and neutrophilic leukocytosis in a diabetic indicates pyogenic liver abscess; the right pleuritic component is sympathetic/diaphragmatic, not primary pneumonia.
expectedNextQuestions: Any diarrhoea, dysentery, or travel to suggest amoebic aetiology?
History of gallstones, biliary colic, or prior biliary intervention?
Any visual symptoms or headache suggesting metastatic Klebsiella seeding?
expectedInvestigations: Image-guided aspiration/drainage with pus Gram stain and culture
regressionAssertions: stewardship antibiotics include ceftriaxone and metronidazole
imaging shows a solitary rim-enhancing hepatic collection without biliary dilatation
